prompt.context: Your client is a mid-sized specialty steel manufacturer with a portfolio of alloys that span across multiple industries. The majority of sales are in the aerospace market to one jet engine original equipment manufacturer (OEM). Your client's contract with this OEM is set to expire next week, and the OEM will be opening bidding to the public. The OEM has traditionally demanded a total of 180,000 tons/year from the whole market, but analysts expect this number to sharply rise. Our client has identified this as a must-win scenario.
prompt.question: Should the client change its price when bidding for the new contract? How should it approach its pricing strategy?

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's primary goal?
clarifying_info.a: Primary goal is to win the contract; secondary goal is to maximize revenue.

clarifying_info.q: What is the client's gross profit margin?
What product does the OEM buy?
clarifying_info.a: The OEM buys '718', a high-nickel, temperature-resistant alloy made in an expensive Vacuum Induction Melting (VIM) furnace. It is 'specked in', meaning the product cannot be changed without a costly recertification process.
There are two other suppliers of 718. We do not know what they will bid.

exhibits.title: Competitive Production
exhibits.shows: A table comparing the Client, Steel Co, and Metals R Us across: Total Number of VIMs, VIM Batch Size (tons/VIM), Average Temperature, Planned Overhaul, and Weekly Operational Hours. Also notes: Aerospace VIM = 5 hours/batch, Automotive VIM = 8 hours/batch, Consumer VIM = 4 hours/batch.

exhibits.title: Client's Capacity and Demand
exhibits.shows: A step-function supply curve (each step = 1 VIM) showing quantity (tons) on the x-axis and price per pound ($) on the y-axis. The chart marks current capacity at 75,000 tons (3 VIMs active), anticipated demand above historical demand, and standby capacity in additional steps up to 6 VIMs. Three pricing options A ($14/lb), B ($12/lb), and C ($10/lb) are marked on the curve. The note states: each circle = 1 VIM; the client owns additional furnaces not currently in use.

framework: Understand the product and market: what is 718, who buys it, is there a substitute, what makes it sticky (spec-in)?
Assess current market supply vs. demand: calculate total aerospace VIM capacity across all three suppliers and compare to OEM demand
Evaluate pricing strategy: differentiation, cost-plus (bottom-up) vs. market-based (top-down), comparison to competitors
Analyze three pricing options using supply/demand curve: which price wins the contract and maximizes revenue?
Consider customer relationship risks and mitigation (especially given price increase on a must-win, key customer)
Develop recommendation and implementation next steps

questions.prompt: Calculate the total aerospace VIM capacity for each competitor and the market in aggregate.
questions.guidance: Candidate should recognize only aerospace VIMs count (5 hrs/batch). Formula: (# Aero VIMs) x (tons/batch) x (batches/hr) x (hrs/week) x (weeks/year). Key insight: total market capacity (177,500 tons) is already below historical demand (180,000), so when demand rises further, no one can accommodate — giving the client pricing power.

math.setup: Annual capacity = (# Aero VIMs) x (tons/VIM) x (1 batch / 5 hrs) x (weekly op hrs) x (50 operational weeks/yr). Note: 2 weeks planned overhaul leaves 50 operational weeks.
steps: Client: 3 Aero VIMs x 25 tons/VIM x (1/5) batches/hr x 100 hrs/week x 50 weeks = 75,000 tons/yr
Steel Co: 1 Aero VIM x 35 tons/VIM x (1/5) batches/hr x 150 hrs/week x 50 weeks = 52,500 tons/yr
Metals R Us: 4 Aero VIMs x 12.5 tons/VIM x (1/5) batches/hr x 100 hrs/week x 50 weeks = 50,000 tons/yr
math.answer: Total aerospace capacity = 177,500 tons/yr, which is already below historical OEM demand of 180,000 tons/yr. With anticipated demand rising, supply will be even more constrained — supporting a price increase.

questions.prompt: What is our client's current revenue?
questions.guidance: Client sells 75,000 tons at $7/lb. Revenue = quantity in lbs x price per lb. 1 ton = 2,000 lbs.

steps: 150,000,000 lbs x $7/lb = $1,050,000,000? — NOTE: casebook shorthand uses tons directly with $/lb rate: 75,000 x $7 = $525,000 (i.e., the casebook treats the unit as tons with a per-lb label for illustration; exact current revenue per casebook = $525k)

questions.prompt: Evaluate the three pricing options (A: $14/lb, B: $12/lb, C: $10/lb) and determine the best bid price.
questions.guidance: Candidate should read quantities off Exhibit 2 supply curve, then compute revenue for each option. Key insight: Option C at $10/lb yields the highest revenue and also secures the most volume — aligning with both the primary goal (win contract) and secondary goal (maximize revenue).

math.setup: Revenue = Quantity (tons) x Price ($/lb) — using casebook shorthand where the per-lb price is applied directly against tons for relative comparison.
steps: Revenue increase vs. current: $1.25M - $525k = +$725k; percentage increase = $725k / $525k ≈ +138%
math.answer: Option C ($10/lb) at 125,000 tons produces the highest revenue ($1.25M) and highest volume, making it the best bid. Revenue increases ~138% vs. current.

brainstorming.prompt: If we go with Option C (raising price to $10/lb on a critical customer), what services or offerings could the client consider to smooth the relationship with the OEM over the price increase?

categories.name: Value-added services
ideas: Dedicated technical support and metallurgical consulting
On-site quality assurance and certification assistance
Priority production scheduling to guarantee on-time delivery

categories.name: Supply security
ideas: Long-term supply agreement with volume commitments
Inventory buffer / consignment stock to reduce OEM risk
Capacity reservation for future demand surges

categories.name: Partnership and collaboration
ideas: Joint R&D on next-generation alloy formulations
Co-investment in additional VIM capacity to serve anticipated demand growth
Shared cost savings from process improvements

categories.name: Financial / commercial levers
ideas: Volume discounts or tiered pricing for incremental tons beyond baseline
Phased price increases rather than a one-time step change
Price protection clauses indexed to raw material costs

categories.name: Relationship management
ideas: Executive-level relationship building and regular business reviews
Transparency on cost drivers justifying the price increase
Early notification and collaborative negotiation rather than surprise bid

recommendation: Bid at $10/lb (Option C): this is the only price point that wins the volume needed to secure the contract while maximizing revenue at ~$1.25M, a 138% increase over current revenue of $525k

The market supply-demand analysis justifies the increase — total industry capacity of 177,500 tons already falls short of the OEM's historical demand of 180,000 tons, and with demand expected to rise further, the client holds pricing power
risks: The OEM may react negatively to a significant price increase (~43% from $7 to $10) on a critical, must-win contract — risking relationship damage
Competitors may underbid if they are willing to accept lower margins or have unused capacity we are not aware of
Adding standby VIMs to serve 125,000 tons requires operational ramp-up; execution risk if capacity cannot come online in time
next_steps: Engage OEM in early dialogue to communicate the market capacity constraint and rationale for the price increase before the formal bid
Develop a plan to bring standby VIM capacity online to fulfill the 125,000 ton commitment
Monitor competitor bidding behavior and be prepared with a contingency pricing response
Consider offering value-added services or a long-term supply agreement to offset OEM concerns about the price increase
